hero.p1: I design by thinking about how something is used first, not just how it looks — a lens I bring from my background in product design. My technical foundation in frontend lets me work end to end: from wireframe to functional component.
hero.p2: Bilingual technical support taught me to listen for what people actually need, beyond what they say.
hero.p3: I'm detail-oriented down to what barely shows. Like salt: you notice when it's missing.

bio.p1: I started designing objects you can touch, and ended up designing interfaces you can use — the thread between the two never changed: understanding first who what I make is for.
bio.p2: That curiosity doesn't stay at work: I care about how people experience things, whether physical, digital, or entirely intangible. I'd rather that show in what I do than in what I say.

woof.tagline: A character-driven e-commerce for BARF dog food

s1.title: Context
s1.p: An e-commerce project built by a cross-functional team of 8 during a 6-week bootcamp. My role: UX Lead — brand identity, design system, packaging, site structure and flows, Figma prototyping, and part of the frontend implementation.

s2.title: The problem
s2.p: Pet owners in the Mexico City metro area looking for BARF food options run into visually generic brands with nothing to set them apart. The challenge was to create a platform that conveyed trust and character at once — without falling into the “cute”, department-store look that dominates the category.

s3.title: Design decisions
s3.p1: The husky in sunglasses was no accident: it ties raw food to the wolf, its natural origin, while the glasses give the brand the “cool” personality that sets it apart from more conventional competitors. The same thinking guided the color system — I chose tones that felt “food-like” without giving up the meaning we already expect from certain colors (green for positive, red for error), and documented full variations in Figma so the team could apply them consistently.
s3.p2: On the packaging, the transparent window isn't a random shape: embracing a “cool”, tough identity, I designed the cut-out to look as if the pack had been “torn open”. Each size has its own mascot (different breeds) and the same ingredients that appear in the site's hero, so the brand feels the same wherever you meet it.

g1.title: Brand identity and packaging
g1.p: I designed the full identity: logo, color system, typography (refined through team feedback), and application rules for social media, labeling and advertising in different formats. I also designed the packaging, iterating through several versions to reach the final one. The ingredient and dish compositions were built with AI as a style reference for the additional mascots; I organized, separated and adapted them to the brand identity.

g2.title: Website
g2.p: I designed the site's structure and flows — not just the Figma screens but the entire journey — the header and footer with feedback from my teammates, and the sign-in and sign-up flow, which I implemented in code together with a teammate (HTML5 + CSS3). I also coordinated visual consistency across the pages the rest of the team built: alignment, colors and styles. On the home page, the husky stays still while dishes and ingredients orbit around it; they stop on hover and link to the catalog on click.
g2.credits: Team credits: the “About us” section (with cards that flip on hover) was my teammates' idea and build; I only recreated it in Figma to keep it in the file. The home animation adapts a concept I saw on another site (a pug with information cards around it). The catalog filters were implemented by another teammate; my contribution was the visual proposal. I also designed the “My account” section in Figma, which fell outside the final scope due to time.

g3.title: Process
g3.p: From wireframes to a connected prototype in Figma.

s5.title: Reflection
s5.p: We did not run formal user research. On a real project, I would have validated the value proposition with at least 5 interviews with pet owners before defining the visual identity. I would also have reduced the background visual noise on secondary pages to improve content legibility.

xanat.tagline: App and website to protect endangered flora

s1.title: Context
s1.p: Solo project completed in 6 weeks as one of the three capstone projects of the Google UX Design Certificate (Coursera). Xanat is a fictional organization focused on the protection, propagation and care of endangered flora in Mexico. My role: UX designer in charge of conceiving and designing the app and the responsive website, end to end.

s2.title: The problem
s2.p: More than 60 species native to Mexico are endangered because of habitat destruction, introduced non-native species and pests — an imbalance that also pushes pollinators toward vulnerable areas. The challenge: design a tool that educates people about caring for these species, improves quality of life for those involved, and supports the farming communities that depend on them.

s3.title: Research process
s3.p1: I reviewed the theoretical framework from sources such as SAGARPA and UNAM's Botanical Garden to build the interview questions. Participation from real users was limited — mostly family members — and was complemented with simulated interviews as part of the exercise. Even with that limitation, the finding was clear: most people didn't know how many or which species are endangered, but were willing to help if they had a simple tool to guide them.
s3.p2: With those findings I ran an ideation exercise focused on education and guidance — how to bring these species into the daily life of someone with no prior knowledge — and defined the information architecture with a sitemap (Garden, Nursery, Cart, About) that later guided every screen.

g1.title: From paper to prototype
g1.p: I started with paper sketches, then digital wireframes and a low-fidelity prototype for the usability tests.

g2.title: What the tests changed
g2.p: The results changed concrete decisions: the home screen stopped showing the status of the newly added plant and instead presents slides about plant care, farming communities and news on species-protection progress, and I added a “buy” option on the species pages (as seed, plant or derivative, depending on each species' legal conditions).

g3.title: High fidelity and responsive design
g3.p: I built the high-fidelity prototype keeping the same flow, and designed the product in three formats — mobile website, mobile app and desktop website — with clear typographic hierarchy and labels designed for screen readers.

s5.title: Reflection
s5.p: Users who tried the prototype said the language and layout felt friendly, even for a topic that might seem meant only for specialists. What I learned: even when the problem is big, working through each step of the process with discipline and adjusting to people's needs helps find viable, useful solutions. With more time, I would run another round of usability tests to validate the changes, add more engaging ways to keep users interested, and reach out to more farming communities.
